title: Xiongnu
fact_summary: A steppe people of Inner Asia known from Chinese sources. Genetic studies on this map compare Hun-period and conqueror-period graves with them.

claims.text: A 2019 study calls them “Inner Asian Xiongnus” and says that “Recent genetic data connect European Huns” to them.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the study reports, read in the open copy linked under Sources.

claims.text: A 2022 study refers to “the disappearance of Xiongnus from Chinese sources” when discussing where the Huns came from.
claims.certainty_reason: A passing remark; the Chinese sources themselves are not cited here.

claims.text: The same 2022 study counts “descendants of late Xiongnus” among the ancestors of the conquering Hungarians' immigrant core.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the study reports, read in the open copy linked under Sources.

claims.text: A 2025 study calls the Xiongnu “the founders of the first nomadic empire of the Mongolian steppe” and says their empire dissolved about 300 years before the Huns appeared in Europe.
claims.certainty_reason: The study's summary of the background, not its own finding; the works it cites have not been opened.

claims.text: The same study finds many long shared DNA segments between 5th–6th-century people of the Carpathian Basin and people of the late Xiongnu period, and concludes that the ancestors of the Hun-period group “are at most a few hundred years away from the late Xiongnu group”.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the study reports, read in the open copy linked under Sources.

open_questions.text: When and where do the Chinese sources stop mentioning the Xiongnu? A 2025 study speaks of a gap of about 300 years before the Huns appear in Europe; the Chinese sources themselves have not been read.

review.note: Checked by Claude against open copies of every source. Marc spot-checks a sample.
